 November 20, 2026 | Reviewed by Joe Ashwell
 First reported on New Civil Engineer 
 30 Second Briefing
 Flood damage costs in England could be up to 11 times higher by 2125 if current levels of investment in flood defences are not maintained, according to a new Environment Agency assessment. The analysis models long‑term climate change impacts on fluvial and coastal flooding and compares outcomes under sustained versus reduced capital and maintenance spending on embankments, barriers and drainage networks. For civil and geotechnical engineers, the findings signal sustained demand for upgraded floodwalls, raised defences and improved surface water management to keep residual risk within acceptable economic and safety thresholds.
 Technical Brief
 Uncertainties in climate projections, socio-economic growth and asset deterioration rates constrain precision of long-range damage estimates.
 Our Take
 The Environment Agency features heavily across recent Hazards coverage, including drought and PFAS river quality pieces, underscoring that long-term flood-damage projections for England sit alongside parallel water-stress and contamination pressures for the same regulator.
 With political moves reported to abolish the Environment Agency and Natural England, a projected 11-fold rise in flood damage by 2125 gives local authorities and infrastructure owners a quantitative risk argument for retaining or replacing statutory oversight rather than devolving responsibility piecemeal.

 Related Articles
 Hazards about 1 hour ago HSE data: 25 construction deaths in 2025/26 – CDM and site risk lessons for engineers
 Construction recorded 25 worker fatalities in 2025/26, the highest of any UK industry, out of 126 workplace deaths reported in provisional Health and Safety Executive (HSE) data. Although detailed causation is not yet published, the figures keep construction disproportionately represented relative to its workforce share, reinforcing the need to control known high-risk activities such as work at height, lifting operations and temporary works. Contractors and clients can expect continued HSE scrutiny on CDM compliance, site supervision quality and design-stage risk elimination.
 Hazards 1 day ago NCE Floods & Water Awards: 21-category snapshot for flood risk engineers
 Entries have opened for New Civil Engineer’s inaugural Floods & Water Awards, featuring 21 categories spanning project delivery, technical innovation and long-term community impact in flood and water management. Categories cover areas such as flood risk schemes, drainage and SuDS, asset resilience, digital tools and data-led decision-making, and organisational or individual contributions. The programme gives geotechnical, civil and water engineers a platform to benchmark approaches to flood defence design, catchment-scale planning and resilience upgrades against UK best practice.
 Hazards 9 days ago South London partial building collapse: stability lessons for urban engineers
 Residents of 14 properties evacuated after the partial collapse of three terraced houses in south London have been allowed back home more than 11 weeks after the incident. Structural engineers have evidently deemed the remaining buildings stable enough for reoccupation following inspections and temporary works to secure the damaged terrace. The case underlines the time and access constraints that follow even localised collapse events, with extended exclusion zones needed while assessing party wall integrity, shared foundations and potential progressive failure in dense urban streets.
